To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the variability of GDP, induced by productivity shocks, is mainly determined by the degree to which the economy is dominated by a few sectors (i.e. the Herfindahl industrial concentration index) but also by the centrality of the economy (i.e. standard deviation of second order degrees), after controlling for the correlation between the two variables.
the variability of GDP is mainly driven by sectoral concentration and, secondarily, by sectoral connectivity.
the propagation of sectoral shocks is determined by the degree and the centrality of inter-industrial linkages, but the former is much more important than the latter.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the analysis of the propagation of productivity shocks in the economy, with a view to assessing the impact of sectoral shocks on the GDP and on the distribution of the welfare across the different sectors.
a new approach to the issue of macroeconomic variability induced by sectoral productivity shocks.
a novel application of a stochastic simulation approach to a global input-output model in the analysis of the propagation of domestic sectoral productivity shocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the propagation of shocks is determined by both the concentration of the economy and its degree of connectivity.

the propagation of domestic sectoral productivity shocks to aggregate output is mainly determined by the degree to which the sector is concentrated, but that the degree of connectivity is also significant, although not as much as concentration.
the degree of industrial centrality is a significant factor in the variability of aggregate output, but that the degree of sectoral concentration has the dominant effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the propagation of productivity shocks depends on the degree of industrial fragmentation.
the more the economy is concentrated and the more the economy has a central position in the network of input–output linkages, the higher the variability of the economy.

the degree of industrial centrality, as measured by the standard deviations of the second-order degrees, plays a minor role, while industrial concentration, as measured by industrial value added, plays a major role in the variability of the economy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degree of centrality of a sector, measured in terms of its second-order connectivity, is a key determinant of the propagation of sectoral shocks to the aggregate level.
the aggregate sensitivity to sectoral shocks depends mainly on the degree of concentration of the productive system.
the variability of GDP, due to productivity shocks, is determined by the degree to which the economic system is concentrated and by its connectivity, with the latter being a less significant factor.
